engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that a capable system would acquire other objectives before it learns the intended values.

evidence.passage: We will not suddenly be surprised by the existence of such super intelligences. They will evolve technologically over time, and our world will be different, populated by many other intelligences, and we will have lots of experience already.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that instilling ethics is harder than achieving the intelligence that is assumed.

statement: Davis's review of Bostrom's Superintelligence, dated October 2014, disputes the view that giving a computer an ethical point of view is especially difficult, arguing that an AI able to understand human morality could be told to follow it.
qualification: The review proposes a minimal ethical standard and states that it is impossible until an AI with a very powerful understanding exists; it does not report an implemented method.

evidence.passage: I discuss a number of flaws in his analysis, particularly the viewpoint that implementing ethical behavior is an especially difficult problem in AI research.
If the AI can understand human morality, it is hard to see what is the technical difficulty in getting it to follow that morality.

engagement.rationale: Models developer incentives directly and finds that the incentive to win pushes precautions down.

statement: Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman's technical report of 2013 presents a model in which teams racing to build a powerful AI are incentivised to skimp on safety precautions, and in which more teams and more enmity between them increase the danger of an AI disaster.
qualification: A stylised game-theoretic model with assumptions the authors state (a powerful AI built by the winning team, a disaster probability rising as precautions fall); it does not measure any developer's incentives.

evidence.passage: each team is incentivised to finish first – by skimping on safety precautions if need be.
Having extra development teams and extra enmity between teams can increase the danger of an AI-disaster

statement: Yudkowsky's post of 20 October 2017 states that AlphaGo Zero's progress to a strongly superhuman level at Go, after three days of self-play within about two years of a time when no program had come close to beating a professional, is evidence for his side of the AI-foom debate with Hanson, and that fast capability gains resembling foom need not require self-improvement.
qualification: The post treats a narrow, closed domain (Go) as evidence about general capability gains and says so ('AlphaGo clearly isn't a general AI'). It holds the earliest-located role only through its use of the name “foom” for the transition, not through a stated period (the Go comparison spans two years, and the three days are of self-play in Go). It is the author's reading of one result, not a measurement of general takeoff speed. Texts by Yudkowsky already recorded on A4 (Hard Takeoff, 2008; Intelligence Explosion Microeconomics, 2013) are linked.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "Sheer speed of capability gain"
evidence.passage: Go play went from “nobody has come close to winning against a professional” to “so strongly superhuman they’re not really bothering any more” over two years … says you don’t even need self-improvement to get things that look like FOOM.

engagement.rationale: It states that there is no fundamental limit at human level, without engaging a named argument for a plateau.

statement: Bengio and twenty-three co-authors' paper of October 2023 states that there is no fundamental reason why AI progress would slow or halt at the human level, noting that AI already surpasses humans in narrow domains and is increasingly used to improve AI systems.
qualification: A multi-author consensus paper; the record states what the paper says, not each author's view. Read in arXiv v1; the revised Science version of 2024 was not compared.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 2, opening section, paragraph continuing from p. 1
evidence.passage: There is no fundamental reason why AI progress would slow or halt at the human level.

engagement.rationale: Disputes that AI catastrophe scenarios warrant concern, by arguing that they are imagined without probabilities and assume a will to dominate that intelligence does not entail.

statement: Pinker's Edge response of 2014 argues that there are reasons not to worry about killer robots and machines running amok: disaster scenarios are cheap to play out in the imagination, where no probabilities apply, and AI dystopias project a dominance psychology onto intelligence.
qualification: The response speaks of machines running amok and of disaster scenarios, not of extinction in those words. Recorded after the same-family audit, which named it as earlier than Hawkins (2015); the Edge responses carry no dates of their own. Paraphrase because Pinker's 526-word response already has 48 quoted words.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response by Steven Pinker, paras. 1–2 and 4
evidence.passage: Pinker writes that besides the distance to human-level AI there are other reasons not to worry about killer robots and machines running amok: disaster scenarios are cheap to play out in a probability-free imagination and always find an audience, and AI dystopias project a parochial alpha-male psychology onto the concept of intelligence.

statement: Ngo's report of August 2022 states that by default AGIs seem likely to end up pursuing goals undesirable to humans, and that the lack of formal frameworks for describing alignment problems is a major reason to expect them to be difficult to solve.
qualification: The author states that the argument is uncertain and that problems of the earlier phases are more likely to be solved by default as machine learning progresses; the record is the report's argument, not evidence that alignment is unsolved.

evidence.passage: By default, it seems likely to me that AGIs will end up pursuing goals which are undesirable to us, rather than consistently following our intentions.
our lack of formal frameworks for describing alignment problems is a major reason to expect them to be difficult to solve
I expect that the problems in the earlier phases are more likely to be solved by default as the field of ML progresses

statement: Russell's Edge response of 2014 states that a system's utility function may not be aligned with human values, which are very difficult to pin down, that this is not a minor difficulty, and that AI research, which has aimed at better decisions whatever the utility function, needs to change its goals to building intelligence provably aligned with human values.
qualification: The response states that there is cause for optimism if alignment is treated as intrinsic to AI; it argues for a change in the field's goals, not that alignment cannot be achieved. Earliest located after the same-family audit, which found it among the pack's sources; the Edge responses carry no dates of their own. The second item is a paraphrase because the response's quotation limit is nearly reached.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response "Of Myths And Moonshine", paragraph after the numbered points
evidence.passage: This is not a minor difficulty.

evidence.locator: Same response, numbered point 1 and closing paragraphs
evidence.passage: Russell writes that the values of the human race are at best very difficult to pin down, that improving decision quality irrespective of the utility function has been the mainstream goal of AI research, and that the right response is to change the field's goals to building intelligence provably aligned with human values.

statement: The statement of 31 March 2023 by Gebru, Bender and McMillan-Major states that the harms of AI are real and present, that the pause letter addresses none of them, and that concern should focus on the practices of the companies building the systems rather than on imaginary "powerful digital minds".
qualification: The statement answers the FLI letter; its list of present harms is its own. It records what the statement says, not each author's views elsewhere.

evidence.passage: The harms from so-called AI are real and present and follow from the acts of people and corporations deploying automated systems.
the focus of our concern should not be imaginary "powerful digital minds."

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that one small project could improve software across the full range of mental modules faster than the rest of the world.

statement: Hanson's post of 24 July 2014 argues that a 'local explosion', in which one small project's machine goes within weeks from weaker than a human to able to take over the world, is implausible, because one project could not innovate across thousands of software modules vastly faster than the rest of the world.
qualification: The post contests the single-project, weeks-long form of the proposition; it accepts that machines may eventually do most mental tasks better and may greatly raise economic growth rates. Hanson's earlier posts in the debate with Yudkowsky (2008–2013) are in the dataset and are linked, not re-recorded; this is the earliest located contesting record within the pack's own searches, not before them.

evidence.passage: a single machine, built by a single project using only a tiny fraction of world resources, goes in a short time (e.g., weeks) from being so weak that it is usually beat by a single human … to so powerful that it easily takes over the entire world.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "Similarly, while you might imagine"
evidence.passage: So I can’t see a plausible way one project could increase its intelligence vastly faster than could the rest of the world.

statement: Bostrom's paper of 2012 states the orthogonality thesis: that intelligence and final goals are orthogonal axes along which possible agents can freely vary, so that more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal.
qualification: Earliest located among the texts this group's search found that meet the criterion with an attested date; it is not evidence of coinage. The paper states the thesis 'with some caveats' and holds that it concerns logical possibility, not that arbitrary goals would be easy to instil.

evidence.locator: Section 1.2, The orthogonality thesis, PDF p. 3
evidence.passage: Intelligence and final goals are orthogonal axes along which possible agents can freely vary. In other words, more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal.

The orthogonality thesis suggests that we cannot blithely assume that a superintelligence will necessarily share any of the final values stereotypically associated with wisdom and intellectual development in humans

statement: Goertzel and Pitt's paper of February 2012 states that the authors believe, on qualitative grounds, that an open approach to developing artificial general intelligence is probably preferable to a closed one, citing the wider critique an open codebase receives.
qualification: The paper concerns open-source AGI code and development, before model weights were the object of the debate; the authors say they do not argue the point rigorously and name the risk of malevolent groups forking an open project. A statement of the authors' intuition, not evidence that open development is safer.

evidence.locator: Section 2, "Is open or closed AGI development safer?"
evidence.passage: We do believe intuitively that the open approach is probably preferable, but our reasons are qualitative and we recognize there are also qualitative arguments in the opposite direction.
The authors cite Linus's law ("Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow") and write that a closed approach makes it very hard to obtain the level of critique a public, open codebase receives.
we also understand the risk of terrorist groups or other malevolent agents forking an open source AGI project and creating something terribly dangerous and destructive

engagement.rationale: It disputes the counting argument, the premise that more possible goals are compatible with scheming than with alignment.

statement: Belrose and Pope's essay of February 2024 argues that the counting argument for scheming in Carlsmith's report rests on an incorrect application of the principle of indifference, and that once the principle is rejected there is very little reason left to expect future AIs to become schemers.
qualification: Records the essay's critique of one argument for scheming; it does not report evidence about trained systems' goals.

evidence.passage: they rest on an incorrect application of the principle of indifference
Once we reject the indifference principle, there is very little reason left to worry that future AIs will become schemers.

statement: Pinker's Edge response of 2014 argues that superhumanly intelligent robots would have no reason to want to depose their masters or dominate, because goals are extraneous to intelligence and dominance-seeking is a product of primate natural selection, not a feature of intelligent systems.
qualification: Earliest located among the texts this group's search found; the Edge responses carry no dates of their own. The passage also states that goals are extraneous to intelligence, which is the independence that R01 asserts.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response by Steven Pinker, para. 4
evidence.passage: Even if we did have superhumanly intelligent robots, why would they want to depose their masters, massacre bystanders, or take over the world?

statement: Bostrom's paper of March 2002 states that a small group in control of the initial superintelligence could conceivably select its goals and form a world government reflecting only the idiosyncratic values of its owners or designers, which, depending on those values, the paper would count as an existential catastrophe (a "shriek").
qualification: The passage concerns the deliberate selection of a superintelligence's goals by a small group to entrench its values; it names no weapon or attack, and it presents the scenario as conceivable, not likely. Recorded on R09 for the seizure or entrenchment of power the criterion names.

evidence.passage: Such a world government could conceivably be formed by a small group of people if they were in control of the first superintelligence and could select its goals.
the posthuman world may reflect only the idiosyncratic values of the owners or designers of this superintelligence.

engagement.rationale: States that domination-seeking comes from evolved psychology, without addressing the argument that it would arise instrumentally from other goals.

statement: Pinker's Edge response of 2014 argues that megalomaniacal behaviour is a product of natural selection in one primate species, not an inevitable feature of intelligent systems.
qualification: Earliest located among the contesting records on R02 found by this search, by page order within the undated 2014 discussion. The passage does not discuss the argument that power or resources would be sought as means to other goals.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response by Steven Pinker, para. 4
evidence.passage: these are products of a history of natural selection shaping testosterone-sensitive circuits in a certain species of primate, not an inevitable feature of intelligent systems.

statement: Brooks's blog post of November 2014 argues that worry about malevolent AI rests on a misunderstanding of how far the field is from volitional machines, and calls worrying about intentionally evil AI fear mongering and a waste of time.
qualification: The argument concerns "malevolent" or "intentionally evil" AI and the time scale of human-level AI (the post says centuries); it does not address risk from systems that harm without intent. Read in a same-month repost, not in the original.

evidence.passage: I think it is a mistake to be worrying about us developing malevolent AI anytime in the next few hundred years.
Worrying about AI that will be intentionally evil to us is pure fear mongering. And an immense waste of time.
